text:
Step-by-step how to generate 20M+ impressions per year on LinkedIn:

(adding $5,000,000 in new ARR along the way)

1. Identify who your ideal buyer is

Sounds obvious, but lots of creators make 'viral' content that doesn't convert.

They post about what they deem interesting and end up educating their competitors rather than their target buyers.

For example, I want GTM Leaders to consume my content. 
It's purposefully NOT made for GTM agencies (my competitors).


2. Identify who shall see your content

GTM leaders might be your buyers.

But GTM operators could be the ones seeing the content & sharing it with their managers.

It's okay for your content not to be purposefully made for your ideal buyer... as long as there's a path for them to find it.


3. Review what has already been produced

→ Look at your existing content

- How do you make more of the pieces that outperformed, as well as variations of these?

→ Look at your competition content

- How do you make it more advanced, simpler to understand, or more aesthetically pleasing?

→ Look at thought leaders in your niche

- What's the gap in quality between their content & yours? 
- What are the things they're doing better?
- How fast can you close this gap?


4. Uncover proven content ideas/angles

Create a swipe file of outlier content in your niche.

Using tools such as Taplio & Scripe, you can find viral content by 
- specific authors
- through keywords
- in adjacent niches

Think about how these 'proven' posts & formats can be adapted to your subject matter.


5. Identify winning formats

The key to winning at LinkedIn = identifying a combination of proven topic angles + formats that you decline week after week.

That is:
- Finding 2-3 topics to talk about weekly (e.g: ai agents, gtm tech)
- Identifying formats you'll keep using to package your content (e.g: tools carousel, schema infographics)

Content doesn't always need to be new to perform.
It needs to be shown to people who haven't seen it yet.


6. Alternate between TOF, MOF & BOF content pieces.

- Some content should bring new people into your ecosystem (TOF)
- Some should pique interest in your offerings (MOF)
- Some should get them to take action (BOF)

It's rare for a single publication to achieve all 3 at once.
Decide what the goal of your post is.


7. Package your content with nice visual designs

"An image is worth a 1000 words"
... a video is made up of thousands of images.

Attention-grabbing designs always improve reach.


8. Expand the playbook to your team

You can't publish 2+ posts/day without losing out on reach.
But more posts = more overall impressions.

The trick is to get your team to post as well.

For us, that meant 581 posts from 24 different people, which added $151K MRR within 90 days.

(I made a video on how to replace this if you'd like to view it)


P.S. What is your LinkedIn strategy?

text:
How the top 1% actually run cold email in 2026:

(After analyzing 1,000,000+ emails in Instantly.ai)

Here are the patterns that top-performing campaigns had in common:


1. Tight Lists > Broad Lists

Micro-lists of 500-1,000 hyper-targeted prospects crushed 100,000-contact blasts.

Reply rates: 20-30% vs. 2-3%.

→ Stop spraying and praying. Target people who actually have a reason to reply.


2. Hyper-Enriched Data > Standard Data

Don't settle for name + email. Pull:

- Tech stack
- Social activity
- Funding rounds
- Current initiatives
- Website case studies
- LinkedIn headline & profile
- Job postings (hiring/growth signals)

→ Real 'personalization at scale' begins with deep enrichment.


3. Personalized Openers > Generic Openers

Instead of: "Hey John, hope all's well at [Company]"

Try:
- Job postings → "Saw you're expanding your GTM team for [initiative]"
- Tech stack → "Noticed you recently added [tool]…"
- Case studies → "Just read your case study on…"

→ Every email should feel 1:1.


4. 3-Step Sequence > Single Email

Most replies land on the first email, but follow-ups dramatically lift overall sequence reply rates.

- Email 1: Personalized opener + upfront value
- Email 2: Fresh new angle (3-5 days later)
- Email 3: Last attempt (3-5 days later)

→ Keep them short (2-4 sentences). Reference the first. Add new value.

Pro tip: Layer LinkedIn touches between emails.


5. Value-First > Ask-First

Stop pitching a slot in their calendar in email 1.

❌ "Can we hop on a call tomorrow at 2pm?"
❌ "Do you have 15 minutes to chat?"

✅ "Want me to send over a quick example deck?"
✅ "Happy to share what's working right now."
✅ "Can I send you something that could solve [specific pain]?"

→ Let them raise their hand first. Earn the conversation.


6. Fundamentals > Fancy Tactics

Nail the 3 core pillars:

1. ICP = who exactly are you targeting?
2. Offer = what outcome do you deliver?
3. Copy = how do you communicate value?

→ Depth > width. Skip the shiny objects.


7. Deliverability > Volume

None of the above matters if you land in spam.

Deliverability rules:
- Clean, validated lists
- Multiple domains (not one)
- 30-day minimum warm-up
- 20 emails per inbox per day max
- Proper setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)

→ 100 emails/hour from one inbox = straight to spam.


8. Tech Stack

- Instantly.ai (sequencing, deliverability, analytics)
- Claude Code (orchestration, enrichment)
- Attention (meeting recording)


Want to go deeper? 👇

Check out the Cold Email cheat sheet below.

text:
I used Naga's content system to generate 8.4M impressions on X/Twitter in under 6 months.

And crazy enough… it runs entirely via Claude Code.

He was kind enough to show me what's under the hood 👇


1️⃣ One agent runs everything

Naga built a single content agent that acts as the orchestrator.

It connects to 3 things: Notion (memory), Apify (post monitoring), Slack (updates).

His tweets, threads, long-form articles are all produced end-to-end from one terminal.


2️⃣ The memory layer is what makes it smart

Any AI system is only as good as its data. 
So the memory holds:

- Client profiles (everything public & verifiable about you)
- Content library (every past post across LinkedIn, X, YouTube)
- Draft memory (so it never recycles the same ideas)
- Idea bank (every concept from past ideation sessions)
- Sentinel intel (inspiration accounts it tracks for winning patterns)

It all gets consolidated into a cache, so the agent only pulls the most relevant data, and output quality never slips.


3️⃣ Skills give it your voice

For each client, the agent invokes specific skills:

- A writing skill (trained on your posts + proven copywriting frameworks)
- A voice profile (tone, phrases, energy, so it never sounds like a machine)
- An algo scorer 


4️⃣ It scores every idea against the real algorithm

X open-sourced its full ranking algorithm on GitHub.

Naga forked it and built an algo scorer that ranks each content idea (S-tier, A-tier…) on:

- Bookmark probability
- Reply magnetism
- Hook velocity

Then it cross-references theory against what's actually working on your account.


5️⃣ Human judgment stays in the loop

The agent ideates, scores, and flags.

text:
How to get 30%+ reply rates with LinkedIn DMs:

(Based on 200+ pitches that hit my inbox this month)

Context: I've sent 10M+ outbound messages last year via my $7M ARR GTM agency.

Now? 
I spend more time cleaning my inbox than launching campaigns.

I'm the Founder & CEO of a 37-person company.
Like many execs, I open and reply to cold DMs.

In an ideal world, I'd reply to most DMs...
But I don't.

Here's how I decide whether I reply or not…

And... how I rebuilt my own LinkedIn DM frameworks around it 👇


✅ DMs offering *free* work

Some people offered to rewrite our landing pages.
Others offered to draft sample scripts for my YouTube.

During ColdIQ's early days, we'd run campaigns giving away custom lead lists for free…
And we'd get way more replies than we'd know what to do with.

Pro tip: Imagine the prospect already signed as a client. 
What's the first thing you'd ship for them? Do it already, for free.


✅ DMs that ask for an internal referral

If you've actually researched what we're working on at ColdIQ and found out who owns it, I'll happily route you to the right person.

Pro tip: You can scale this play by stacking buying signals inside of Clay with their 'find person' feature to surface a colleague in a specific department.

(Also, my friend Brahim Sliti at LeadsFactory built a live 'find person' feature that catches contacts other tools miss)


❌ DMs asking to 'pick' my brain 

I receive many requests from founders/builders who want feedback on their new tool/startup idea.

I'd love to... but time is tight, and there's little to no upside for me.


✅ DMs w/ actually valuable insights

I published a variation of this post a while back and got a great take from Jihad Iqbal worth sharing 👇

"
The best 'free work' isn't actually work. It's insights.

I send technical audits of prospects' platforms.
→ 5-minute analysis
→ 3 specific optimization opportunities
→ No strings attached

E.g: 'Your checkout flow has a 23% drop-off at payment verification. Here's why + 2 quick fixes.'

- Takes me 10 minutes.
- Shows instant value.
- Demonstrates expertise without asking for anything.

The key: make it so valuable they'd normally pay for it.

Generic 'free consultation' = everyone does this.
Specific actionable insight = rare.
"

This sort of strategy will always keep working ☝️


❌ DMs with 0 personalization

Plenty of teams still run pure-volume plays, blasting the same template to everyone.

Appealing to everyone = appealing to no one.
You're wasting your DMs.


✅ DMs from 'notorious' people

A bit unfair, but WHO sends the message matters as much as the message itself.

If a public figures in your space (e.g: Alex Hormozi) sent you the worst LinkedIn DM ever… you'd still want to reply.

I watched my own reply rates greatly increase as I built up my personal brand.

Pro tip: If you're in B2B, build up your LinkedIn profile.

I haven't got any space left... more tips in the carousel.

PS. What's the best DM you ever got? Share it below 👇

text:
How to run email outreach like the top 1%:

(Based on 1,000,000+ emails analyzed in Instantly.ai)

Here were the common patterns shared by the highest-performing campaigns:


1. Small Lists > Broad Lists

Micro-lists of 500-1,000 hyper-targeted prospects greatly outperformed 100,000-contact blasts.

Reply rates: 20-30% vs. 2-3%.

→ Stop spraying & hoping someone bites. Target people who actually have a reason to reply.


2. Hyper-Enriched Data > Standard Data

Don't stop at just name + email. Pull:

- Tech stack
- Social activity
- Funding rounds
- Current initiatives
- Website case studies
- LinkedIn headline & profile
- Job postings (hiring/growth signals)

→ Effective 'personalization at scale' starts with deep data enrichment.


3. Personalized Openers > Generic Openers

Instead of: "Hey John, hope all's well at [Company]"

Try:
- Job postings → "Saw you're hiring 3 AEs…"
- Case studies → "Just read your case study on…"
- Tech stack → "Noticed you recently added [tool]…"

→ Every email should feel 1:1.


4. 3-Step Sequence > Single Email

Most replies hit on the first email, but follow-ups massively lift overall sequence reply rates.

- Email 1: Personalized opener + value
- Email 2: New angle (3-5 days later)
- Email 3: Breakup (3-5 days later)

→ Keep them short (2-4 sentences). Reference the first. Add new value.

Pro tip: Layer LinkedIn touches between emails.


5. Value-First > Ask-First

Stop pitching a spot in your prospect's calendar in email 1.

❌ "Can we hop on a call tomorrow at 2pm?"
❌ "Do you have 15 minutes to chat?"

✅ "Want me to send over a quick example deck?"
✅ "Happy to share what's working right now."
✅ "Can I send you something that could solve [specific pain]?"

→ Let them raise their hand first. Earn the conversation.


6. Fundamentals > Fancy Tactics

Nail the 3 core pillars:

1. ICP = who exactly are you targeting?
2. Offer = what outcome do you deliver?
3. Copy = how do you communicate value?

→ Depth > width. Skip the shiny objects.


7. Deliverability > Volume

None of the above advice matters if you land in spam.

Deliverability rules:
- Clean, validated lists
- Multiple domains (not one)
- 30-day minimum warm-up
- 30 emails per inbox per day max
- Proper setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)

→ 100 emails/hour from one inbox = you're landing in spam.


9. Tech Stack

- Instantly.ai (sequencing, deliverability, analytics)
- Clay (enrichment, intent, personalization)
- Prospeo (data, targeting)


Want to learn more? 👇

Check out the Cold Email cheat sheet below.

text:
Your AI Agent spent $4,200 in API credits. 

No one told it to stop.

AI agents are making seat-based pricing obsolete.

It used to make sense:

More people interacting with a product meant more usage.
This justified charging customers higher prices.

But an agent can now interact with software and perform more actions than a team of 100 people.

Thus, you’re charging for 1 seat.
While the agent uses the equivalent of 1,000 seats.

The smartest companies have acted already:

Take a platform like Clay as an example:

Workflow orchestration used to be free.

So people were abusing the *free* actions and plugging their API keys for most data actions.

That meant running 1,000-row automated workflows, free of charge.

When humans were manually setting up these workflows, it wasn’t that big of a deal…

There’s a limit to how much you can *humanly* abuse a product.

But plug your agent to Clay…
Have it build 100s of 1000-row tables.

And now you understand why Clay NEEDED to start charging per action.

On the flip side, usage-based API products are generating more revenue than ever.

When people prompt agents to “build a lead list of VP of Sales in New York” they have no idea how many leads will be found.

Let your agent work autonomously, and all of a sudden, you’re paying for a list of 50,000+ prospects.

Had you performed these actions manually, you’d have realised that building such a list would have cost you a lot. And you’d have stopped the build list before it broke your budget.

But all the steps were performed without your supervision… 
So you now have to pick up the bill.

For API providers, it’s magic:
- Claude Code went crazy & spent all the credits.
- They make the money, but they’re not too blame because “it’s Claude Code’s fault”.

That said:

These pricing models do not work for every SaaS company on earth.

Which is why we’re partnering with Hyperline’s CEO Lucas Bédout to discuss how pricing should evolve in the age of AI.

It’s happening at 2 PM CET, today: https://lnkd.in/eiAaHfvR 

(Don’t miss it!)

text:

What took hours now takes minutes.

The old way:

B) They prospect via email, phone and LinkedIn.

The new way:

A) Specialists own a channel.
B) Systems orchestrate outbound across channels.


What does this mean for SDRs?

1. You double down on human activities.

AI isn't replacing people who are great at cold calling just yet.

In a world where everything can be automated, most will chase shortcuts.

Along with investing more time to:
- Navigate complex deals

You learn to use tools like Clay, Claude Code, PredictLeads, Prospeo, FullEnrich, Common Room, Instantly.ai, lemlist, Relevance AI.

And you push AI to its limits in areas where it completely outperforms humans:

i.e:
- Detecting patterns across millions of data points
- Scoring and researching 10,000 prospects in minutes
- Running dozens of workflows simultaneously without fatigue


The best SDR teams combine both:

- GTM Engineers who build large-scale prospecting systems and feed laser-accurate data to SDRs.

- SDRs who book meetings through manual outreach and the phone.

text:
This LinkedIn strategy helps us generate $19,000+/day.

I helped a $10M/year SaaS founder replicate it in 73 minutes:

Here are some of the tips I gave him 
(that took me from 2K to 69K followers):


1. Treat your profile like a landing page

Your tagline needs social proof.
Your banner must include your value prop, not a vague quote.

2. Get LinkedIn Premium for the custom CTA button

One-click path from your post to your website.
No need to visit your profile first.

3. Post at the exact same time every day

Think of it like a TV show.
Pick a time you'll never miss and stick to it within 10 minutes.

4. Never schedule your posts

Always hit publish manually.
Scheduled posts consistently underperform. I tested it and saw an instant dip.

5. Find 2-3 recurring formats you can decline every week

Proven topic + proven format = consistent performance.
Content doesn't need to be new. It needs to reach people who haven't seen it yet.

6. Build a swipe file of outlier content in your niche

Use tools like Scripe or Taplio.
Filter for top-performing posts by specific creators, keywords, or adjacent niches.

7. Mix "yolo" posts with ICP-targeted posts

Personal storytelling brings people into your ecosystem.
But min. 2 posts per week must address your buyer's pain points directly.

8. Carousels can 2x your impressions

Images take up more space in the feed than text.
More visual real estate = more people stop scrolling.

9. Repost your content 6 hours after publishing

Delete yesterday's repost, publish today's piece, repost it by evening.
This alone adds 15-20% extra reach across different time zones.

10. Repurpose your best hits every 2-3 months

Slightly improve them each time. Add two more tools to your "top 10" list.
The biggest predictor of a post exploding is the same format exploding before.

11. Reply to every comment in the first 30 minutes

Engage for 15 minutes before posting to warm up your account.
Then stay on the post and respond to everyone immediately after.

12. Expand the playbook to your team

You can't publish 2+ posts/day without losing reach.
But 24 people posting added $151K MRR in 90 days for us.

text:
Step-by-step how to generate 20M+ impressions per year on LinkedIn:

(adding $5,000,000 in new ARR along the way)

1. Identify who your ideal buyer is

Sounds obvious, but lots of creators make 'viral' content that doesn't convert.

They post about what they deem interesting and end up educating their competitors rather than their target buyers.

For example, I want GTM Leaders to consume my content. 
It's purposefully NOT made for GTM agencies (my competitors).


2. Identify who shall see your content

GTM leaders might be your buyers.

But GTM operators could be the ones seeing the content & sharing it with their managers.

It's okay for your content not to be purposefully made for your ideal buyer... as long as there's a path for them to find it.


3. Review what has already been produced

→ Look at your existing content

- How do you make more of the pieces that outperformed, as well as variations of these?

→ Look at your competition content

- How do you make it more advanced, simpler to understand, or more aesthetically pleasing?

→ Look at thought leaders in your niche

- What's the gap in quality between their content & yours? 
- What are the things they're doing better?
- How fast can you close this gap?


4. Uncover proven content ideas/angles

Create a swipe file of outlier content in your niche.

Using tools such as Taplio & Scripe, you can find viral content by 
- specific authors
- through keywords
- in adjacent niches

Think about how these 'proven' posts & formats can be adapted to your subject matter.


5. Identify winning formats

The key to winning at LinkedIn = identifying a combination of proven topic angles + formats that you decline week after week.

That is:
- Finding 2-3 topics to talk about weekly (e.g: ai agents, gtm tech)
- Identifying formats you'll keep using to package your content (e.g: tools carousel, schema infographics)

Content doesn't always need to be new to perform.
It needs to be shown to people who haven't seen it yet.


6. Alternate between TOF, MOF & BOF content pieces.

- Some content should bring new people into your ecosystem (TOF)
- Some should pique interest in your offerings (MOF)
- Some should get them to take action (BOF)

It's rare for a single publication to achieve all 3 at once.
Decide what the goal of your post is.


7. Package your content with nice visual designs

"An image is worth a 1000 words"
... a video is made up of thousands of images.

Attention-grabbing designs always improve reach.


8. Expand the playbook to your team

You can't publish 2+ posts/day without losing out on reach.
But more posts = more overall impressions.

The trick is to get your team to post as well.

For us, that meant 581 posts from 24 different people, which added $151K MRR within 90 days.

(I made a video on how to replace this if you'd like to view it)

text:
My cold outreach process that generated 25,000+ leads in 2026

(and got us to $7m ARR with our agency)

1. Build a few relevant audience segments

There are some ‘easy’ targeting wins when you run cold outreach for the first time.

- Companies engaging with your brand
- Companies similar to your best clients
- Companies showing buying intent in your category


2. Map your total addressable market (TAM)

That is, every single company that fits your client criteria.

You can use B2B data sources like: Clay, Wiza & Prospeo to build your account lists according to your chosen criteria (company size, geography, industry)


3. Research your target accounts & segment them into tiers.

- Tier 1 should be your dream clients or perfect fits (similar to your best clients).
- Tier 2 should be good fit clients (similar to orgs you helped).
- Tier 3 should be orgs you believe you can help.

You can prompt AI models within Clay to tier/score accounts, or do it within Claude Code by creating a .md file that includes your scoring criteria to be compared against your account list. 

APIs or tools like PredictLeads, Common Room come very handy here as well.


4. Try reaching your entire TAM every 3-6 months

- For Tier 1 leads: mix manual AE outreach + multichannel engagement = phone (use Nooks) + LinkedIn + email.

Pro tip: make sure to write the first 25-50 messages manually. 
Do the unscalable at first; this is how you’ll uncover patterns you can scale later on.

- For Tier 2 leads: automate multichannel outreach with AI (use Clay + lemlist)

Pro tip: make sure every message is valuable, relevant + personalised to each recipient. Think: “what can I send to my prospect that’ll be helpful to him, even if they ignore me”

(Here I like to think of what’s the first thing I’d do if I were to sign them as clients, and I do it already… for free).

Example: Building a free ‘niche’ lead list for target accounts, with companies/people data of their ideal clients.

- For Tier 3 leads: engage leads at scale with a proper deliverability infrastructure (use Instantly.ai).

Use tier 3 leads as an experimental playground to test out various copywriting frameworks. (Let me know if you’d like to see some high-performing ones; we collected our own list.


5. Respond to positive replies asap.

The faster your replies = the higher your meeting rate.
More meetings = more sales.


6. A few bonus tips:

- The lead list // targeting is the most important element to succeed at cold outreach. Spend most of your time on list building.
- You’re interrupting people’s day whenever you’re reaching out cold. Keep that in mind, make it a ’nice’ interruption (not always possible, but try your best!)
- Implement a proper deliverability setup. The biggest killer of email outreach is messages that land in spam.
- Warm your target accounts. If you have budget, build a target list & run LinkedIn ads to them, so that they won’t be 100% cold when they receive your outreach.


P.S: Anything you’d add?

→ Breathable, structured writing
→ A strong hook
→ A nice visual

Identifying proven topics isn’t easy.
→ We put Taplio & Scripe at their disposal to help the team see what works.

Brainstorming hooks can be hit-or-miss.

Designing visuals takes time.

- Built a posting calendar
- Rewrote posts & hooks.
- Brainstormed ideas

- Shared best practices.

text:
Snowflake hit $4,000,000 ARR with 60% of its pipeline generated by SDRs.

For Snowflake: Marketing, SDRs & Sales sit under ONE SINGLE team.

They ran the experiment for specific regions.

- The ones that did it had up to 46% meeting rates.
- The ones that didn’t do this had 17% meeting rates.

1️⃣ Alignment

Marketing & Sales operate hand in hand.

Marketing collects insights to be leveraged by the sales team.
The sales team executes on them within 2 weeks.

Seems obvious, but truth is most companies have these 2 teams working in silos.


2️⃣ Intelligence

Snowflake leverage signals a lot.
Their rationale is to get in front of prospects as soon as they’re exploring their use cases.

They do that via:

- Third-party intent signals (job changes, funding rounds, web searches)

And further down the funnel via:
- First-party intent signals (product usage, email clicks, website visits).

They rely on tools such as Bombora to detect accounts showing interest in the background. I’d suggest leveraging Clay, PredictLeads or Common Room for this.

Accounts flagged as “high intent” convert 4x better than standard accounts in the CRM.


3️⃣ Activation

When accounts display enough buying intent, Snowflake’s teams deploy their “1-2 punch” play.

That is:

Weeks 1 & 2: ABM team nurtures target accounts with personalised campaigns (ads + emails + dedicated landing pages)

Week 3: SDRs jump in with outbound.

By the time an SDR cold calls a prospect… they’re already not cold anymore.

Result = 36% meeting rates on pre-warmed accounts (vs. 10% on cold)

4️⃣ Engagement

They reach prospects everywhere they are.

→ Calls
→ Cold Emails
→ LinkedIn DMs
→ Custom microsites

True multichannel orchestration.

(I’d suggest leveraging a platform like lemlist to replicate this omnichannel engagement)

5️⃣ Optimisation

They continuously iterate on what works and what doesn’t.

Performance metrics get shared between the teams in bi-weekly alignment meetings.

ABM, SDRs, & AEs are all informed of what works in terms of messaging & targeting.

But they don’t try to attribute who’s responsible for the deal precisely.

Instead, they measure impact at the account level and optimise the entire funnel together.

The outcomes speak for themselves:

→ Deal velocity multiplied by 2.
→ Tier-1 accounts convert 5x better.

… and you don’t need Snowflake’s budget or 200+ SDRs to start executing on it.

text:
How the top 1% make Cold Email work in 2026:

(Based on 1,000,000+ emails analyzed via Instantly.ai)

Here's what the best-performing campaigns had in common:


1. Small Targeted Lists > Big Broad Lists

Micro-lists of 500-1,000 hyper-targeted prospects beat blasting 100,000 contacts every time.

Reply rates: 20-30% vs. 2-3%.

→ Stop praying someone bites. Start targeting the actual people who have a reason to reply.


2. Hyperenriched Data > Basic Data

Go beyond name + email. Collect:

- LinkedIn headline & profile
- Job postings (signals growth/hiring needs)
- Technologies used
- Funding announcements
- Website case studies

→ Personalization at scale requires data at scale.


3. AI Personalization > Generic Openers

Instead of: "Hey John, hope all is well at [Company]"

Try:
- Job postings → "Saw you're hiring 3 AEs..."
- Funding news → "Congrats on the $25M Series B..."
- Case studies → "Just read your case study on..."
- Tech stack → "Noticed you recently added [tool]..."

→ Make every email feel 1:1.


4. 4-Step Sequence > 1 Single Email

Most replies come from the first emails, but follow-ups increase overall sequence reply rates significantly.

- Email 1: Personalized opener + value offer
- Email 2: Short follow-up (3-5 days later)
- Email 3: Different angle (3-5 days later)
- Email 4: Breakup email (3-5 days later)

→ Keep them short (2-4 sentences). Reference the original. Add new value.

Pro tip: Layer in LinkedIn touches between emails for omnipresence.


5. Value-First > Ask-First

Stop asking for their time immediately.

❌ "Can we hop on a call tomorrow at 2pm?"
❌ "Do you have 15 minutes to chat?"

✓ "Would it make sense to send over a quick example deck?"
✓ "Happy to share what's working best right now."
✓ "Can I send you something that could help [specific pain]?"

→ They raise their hand first. Then you've earned the conversation.


6. Fundamentals > Fancy Tactics

Master the 3 core pillars:

1. ICP – Who exactly are you targeting?
2. Offer – What specific outcome do you deliver?
3. Copy – How do you communicate value?

→ Depth > Width. No shiny object syndrome.


7. Long Game > Quick Wins

Cold email isn't a magic pill. It's a compounding client acquisition system.

→ Quality over rushing. Pipeline over quick wins. Be there when they're ready to buy.


8. Deliverability > Volume

None of this matters if you land in spam.

- Multiple domains (not just one)
- 30 emails per inbox per day max
- Proper technical setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
- 30 days minimum warm-up
- Clean, validated lists

→ Sending 100 emails/hour from one email = spam city.


9. Tech Stack

- Instantly.ai (sequencing, deliverability, analytics)
- Clay (data enrichment, intent, personalization)
- Prospeo.io (list building, targeting)

Looking for more details? 👇

Check out the Cold Email cheatsheet below.

P.S: What's working for you right now with cold email?

text:
OK- this is going to sound ridiculous.

But, I’ve made well over $2M from posting infographics on LinkedIn.

… and Ada Beltrán created most of these for me.

So here’s the thing:

My LinkedIn journey started with ‘text-only’ publications.
(Like everyone, I guess).

But early on, I started adding some visuals that I’d make myself.

I’d spend 3 hours creating a 7-page carousel.
For it to not even look pretty.

But crazy enough, this ugly visual was getting me 2-3x the likes & the impressions.

So I figured: “if I can write the exact same thing, but get 3x the engagement by just adding an image… why not do it every single time, right?!”

And so this was the beginning of a journey that led me, & then my team, to flood LinkedIn with infographics of all sorts.

20M+ impressions later, it looks like these visuals are still going strong.

My best explanation for why this performs so well is that ‘text-only’ posts take up very little space in the feed.

What this means is that you only have the first 2 lines of your ‘hook’ to entice people into clicking the “see more” button.

But when you publish a 1050 x 1380 image, it takes up the entire space on the feed. People can’t not see the image, and you can actually use it as a second hook by writing a big title on the image. And if it’s detailed enough, it can stand on its own as a post…

But then, everybody started publishing infographics as well.

So I did something even more ridiculous, which was:

Posting ANIMATED infographics.

So here’s the thing:

An animated infographic serves the same purpose as a static one does.

But it holds attention even more, especially if you speed it up, as it loops on itself, making it look like people are watching it over & over (in LinkedIn's eyes, I guess).

So if you want to tap into extra impressions without much more effort, have a look at the infographic below, breaking down how to create animated infographics (#infographiception).

Then, take your best-performing text post ever.
Add a nice visual to it that ‘respects’ the rules laid out below.

And I’ll bet you’ll be thanking me for how well the post performs ✌️

text:
My LinkedIn content creation process that produced 20M+ impressions in 2025:

(And added $4,000,000 in net ARR this year)

1. Identify who you're selling to.

This might sound obvious, but I see this mistake all the time. 

Creators focus on content they find interesting overall.
They end up educating their competitors rather than their target buyers.

E.g: I want revenue leaders to consume my content. 
It's purposefully NOT designed for other GTM agencies.


2. Identify who you want to see your content.

Revenue leaders might be your target ICP.
But SDRs might be the ones sharing it with their manager.

It's ok for your content to cast a wider net if there's a path for it finding your target buyer.


3. Study what has been produced already.

Look at what your competitors produce.

↳ How do you make it better, easier to understand or nicer to look at?

Look at your own existing content.

↳ How can you make more of the pieces that outperformed, or variations of these?

Look at Thought-Leaders in your niche/industry.

↳ What's the gap in quality between your content & theirs? 

Ask yourself, how can you close this gap?

Are they more knowledgeable than you are... or are they packaging their content better?


4. Find proven content ideas.

Based on point #3. 
Start collecting outlier content in your niche.

Use platforms like Taplio & Scripe to find viral pieces in your niche, or adjacent niches.

Reflect on how these proven formats can be adapted to your expertise.


5. Identify content pillars & recurring formats.

To make content work for you, you'll need to produce a certain quantity.

Find 2-3 topics you'll keep talking about week over week.
Find 2-3 topic formats you'll keep using to package your content.

The key to making content work = identifying a combination of proven topic angles & format that you decline over & over.

The content doesn't need to be new all the time.
It needs to be shown to new people.


6. Alternate between TOF, MOF & BOF pieces.

Some content should bring new people into your ecosystem (TOF).
Some content should pique their interest in your offering (MOF).
Some content should get them to take action (BOF).

It's rare for a content piece to do all these 3 things at once.
Decide what the goal of your piece is.


7. Package your content with nice visuals

An image is worth a thousand words.
A video is thousands of images.

You can't go wrong adding attention-grabbing designs to your written pieces.


BONUS:
- Reply to comments (it helps the algorithms but also gives you a pulse around what your target audience is wondering)
- Plan your content (you get much better results if you know in advance what your week looks like content-wise).
- Stay consistent (most quit before they see results. Don't let that be you).
- Start conversations with 'ideal engagers' (more convos = more sales).


P.S: If you need help building a GTM system that includes high-performing B2B content, send a DM :)

Last month, we collectively published 233 posts.

Here’s what’s worked best for us so far in 2025:


1. Leveraging platforms like Taplio for content ideation

It lets you find publications that outperformed.

It’s the fastest way to understand what ‘good’ posts look like for LinkedIn.

Study hooks, frameworks, formats, and CTAs of all these posts.

Re-use the structure of these ‘winning’ publications, and apply them to your niche.


2. Engaging with other creators

LinkedIn pushes you much more when you actively comment on others’ posts.

Last year, I read an experiment where someone:

- Only commented for a couple of weeks
- Only posted for 2 weeks
- Posted & commented

Obviously, posting & commenting together drove the most profile views and follower growth.

But, interestingly, commenting alone earned them more followers than just posting.

Try commenting under posts from large creators, and look at the impression metrics. These might be higher than on any of your posts.

Also, to boost your posts, try this:
- Comment on others’ posts 30 min before hitting ‘publish’
- Reply to every comment you get within the first 30 minutes.


3. Creating scroll-stopping visuals

Visuals occupy lots of space on the LinkedIn feed.

This significantly improves the odds that people read your posts.

Selfies, schemas, infographics, carousels… all these will multiply the reach of your posts.

We’re making it as easy as possible for our team thanks to our designers (Clara & Ada).


4. Repurposing your best hits

Every couple of months: Have a look at your best-performing posts… and rewrite them slightly better.

Have a look at the biggest LinkedIn content creators.

Check their most viral posts.

You’ll notice, they’ve published them over and over…
And they keep performing!

Most viewers forget your posts.
New followers never saw them.

So take your best post ever.
And publish it again.

text:
How I get > 30% replies via LinkedIn DMs

By doing the opposite of the 100+ weekly pitches I get:

CONTEXT

I sent 5M+ outbound messages for my $6.5M+ ARR Agency.

Nowadays...

Answering DMs costs me more time than running campaigns.

I'm the CEO at a 33-person company.
(I can't imagine how much outreach execs in big orgs get)

That said, I know most execs check their inbox.
And many reply.

Here's how I decide whether I'll respond or not...

And how I changed my own outreach because of this ↓


✅  DMs offering free work

Some DMs offered a free landing page rewrite or samples of already-made work.

I ran prospecting campaigns and pitched free custom lead lists.
(These were getting me more positive replies than I could handle)

My recommendation: Imagine your prospect is an existing client. What's the first thing you'll do for them? Do it already and send it over!


✅ DMs asking to be referred

Let's say you:
1. Send a message based on a current initiative of ColdIQ
2. Searched who is in charge of this initiative.
↳ I'll gladly refer you to said person

PS: You can automate this 'play' via Clay by combining intent signals & retrieving a leader/manager in a specific department.


❌ DMs asking for time on the 1st touchpoint

Meetings are my personal hell.
I'm fighting every day to eliminate as many of them as possible.

If you're "just asking 15 min of my time" to pick my brain, I won't answer.


✅ DMs from ‘known’ people

An unfair truth in cold outreach: $WHO sends a message matters even more than WHAT the message is.

If you're a well-known executive, I'll most likely reply.

I saw this firsthand as I grew my LinkedIn to 60K+ followers...

The exact same message would perform better, without changing anything.

Pro tip: If you sell B2B products, build your brand on LinkedIn.


❌ Generic templated outreach

The only way to make impersonal, generic outreach work is to send at a massive volume (millions of messages).

LinkedIn doesn't allow such volume.

So you'd be better off doing this by email.
Or better yet... not at all.


✅ DMs sharing valuable insights

Jihad explained this better than I could under one of my posts:

"
The best "free work" isn't actually work → it's insights.

I send technical audits of prospects' platforms.
→ 5-minute analysis
→ 3 specific optimization opportunities 
→ No strings attached

Example: "Your checkout flow has a 23% drop-off at payment verification. Here's why + 2 quick fixes."

- Takes me 10 minutes.
- Shows immediate value.
- Demonstrates expertise without asking for anything.

The key: Make it so valuable they'd typically pay for it.

Generic "free consultation" = everyone does this.
Specific actionable insight = rare.
"

Solving prospects' issues before they pay you a dime is the fastest way to gain their trust.


🔘 Videos or Voice Notes

I listen to voice notes or watch videos.

It annoys people.
But if they're well done, they'll grab attention.

What's a DM you receive you could NOT ignore?

Share it 👇

text:
AI agents are replacing human employees.

Funny enough, they operate in very similar ways:

The smartest agents don’t work alone.
They work in teams.

Some behave like assistants.
Others as managers.

And as with any sort of team, there are different ways to structure their collaboration.

To illustrate this:
We can look at how 3 multi-agent setups would handle the same task…

For example: Scheduling a quarter business review with an important client.


1️⃣ Hierarchical setup

A manager agent assigning tasks to its agent team members.

1. The manager receives a task = Schedule a business review.

2. It tells a subordinate agent to check potential times to meet with the clients.

3. Another agent checks product usage from the client. "Has usage recently dropped? Is engagement still strong?"

4. A 3rd agent drafts an email based on client availability & product usage: 

"Hey Achilles, it's been a while - wanted to ensure you're using the product to the fullest. How about a quick chat next week, Wednesday?”

5. The manager reviews everything and sends the email.


2️⃣ 'Human-in-the-Loop' 

A smart assistant tapping your shoulder when needed.

1. The agent drafts the business review email and finds some available times.

2. But… it sees the client gave negative feedback 2 weeks ago.

3. Before sending the email, it asks you: “Do you want to review the email before I send it?"

4. You make small tweaks, and you send it.


3️⃣ 'Sequential' setup

Like a factory or an assembly line where each person does one task and hands it off to the next.

1. 1st Agent asks: "Is a quarterly business review due?" based on the client's last meeting time.

2. 2nd Agent pulls client's usage data.

3. 3rd Agent drafts a short email.

4. 4th Agent sends the email to book the meeting.


So, when should you use which?

As a rule of thumb:

- Hierarchical setups work well for complex, multi-step tasks.

- Human-in-the-loop setups are recommended for high-stakes, sensitive tasks.

- Sequential setups for ordered workflows with clear dependencies.


P.S: What's one process in your team that would run better...
with some smart agents working behind the scenes? 👇

2. I'd direct this ‘visibility’ to a short landing page.

Your brand efforts will gather interest.

Interested visitors will check your site or your social profiles.
You want them to understand asap how you help.

The most effective way I found to do so, is to record a 5-min video sales letter, breaking down your offering.

Some people won’t buy straight away.

For them, I’d suggest creating a lead magnet to grab their email addresses

3. I'd reach out to warm ‘high-fit’ leads.

Many prospects will engage with your content but won’t try to schedule a call

Still, they might be interested.

In this case, I’d suggest reaching out to every prospect who’d make an ideal client but hasn’t messaged you yet.

I recommend writing your first 25-50 messages by hand, before trying to automate.

This could look like:
“Hey {{name}}, seems my post on {{topic}} resonated with you. Are you working on {{potential initiatives}}? Happy to swap notes if that’s helpful.

Working hard is difficult on its own.

text:
We scaled past $6.5M in ARR with Instantly.ai powering ~70% of our cold email sending.

Here are my 5 biggest learnings sending millions of emails:

1. Lead with value

Most cold emailers try to gain something from their recipients: 

"can I ask 15 min of your time?"
"can I pick your brain on {topic}?”

The best cold emailers give.

Here’s how I do so:

I picture myself signing these leads as clients.
And I think about the first thing I’d do for them if I were to sign them.

Then I do it.
For free.

For example: 

I ran a campaign targeting recruiting firms.

I figured the first thing I’d do for them would be to build a list of HR Directors at orgs hiring for 10+ roles.

So, I built the list. 
I sent it to them. 

And I attached a tutorial on how they could build it too.

This got me way more leads than I knew what to do with.


2. Nail your messaging for 1 person.

Every novice cold emailer is obsessed with scale.

They ideate strategies and don’t bother with them if they don’t see a clear path to scale.

With cold emailing, it looks like so:

- They build a huge list.
- Think about messaging that will appeal to everyone.
- & realise that appealing to everyone = appealing to no one.

Here’s what I do:

- I build a list of ~20 people who are a perfect fit.
- I write every single message by hand. 

When you craft these messages manually, you uncover patterns that most miss...

which are data points you can leverage later on to scale.


3. Your lead list is your biggest lever to success.

Novice cold emailers spend too much time thinking about what to write.
And too little time thinking about who they should reach out to.

But, 
Sending your message to the right person > sending a nicely crafted message.

You want to identify people struggling with a problem you can solve.
When you do that, the message writes itself. 

E.g: we ran campaigns for an HR SaaS company that helps with employee churn. 

We looked for targets with poor Glassdoor reviews and low employee tenure.

If both were true, we assumed these companies were a good fit.


4. Deliverability is king

Good deliverability doesn't equate success.
Bad deliverability guarantees your cold email campaigns will fail.

In our case, we make sure to do:

- Warm-up emails
- Secondary domains
- No open rate tracking
- Set up SPF, DKIM, DMARC
- Send < 30 emails/day per mailbox

... and, most importantly, sending emails we’d like to receive.


5. Reply to interested leads ASAP.

Replying fast = a bigger proportion of meetings from your positive replies.

Most cold emailers boast positive replies as a success metric.
That’s actually when the real work begins.

→ Note: Instantly released AI reply agents that monitor & draft personalised replies on your behalf. They can run entirely on autopilot... or with a human in the loop.

text:
LinkedIn Ads added us $80,000+ in new ARR in 2025.

Here's the funnel that books us qualified meetings on autopilot:

Most B2B orgs waste their ad spend because their funnel looks like so, for every prospect type:

Cold Audience → Direct CTA
Warm Audience → Direct CTA
Hot Audience → Direct CTA (Yes, again!)

Here's what we do instead:


1. BUILD TRUST (Top of Funnel)

The goal here = being unignorable.

We use the following formats:

- Document Ads (5-8 pages of pure value)
- Single Image Ads (Pain/Fear Hook + Solution)
- Thought-Leader Mini-Demo Videos (15 to 30s)

No need to sell hard here.
Just have leads stop their scroll and think to themselves:

"They understand me" or "This looks useful"


2. BRING PROOF (Middle of Funnel)

At this point, prospects have seen you a few times already.
They don't trust you just yet.

Thus, it's time to show receipts:

Build retargeting audiences with everyone who engaged (i.e: website visit, viewed half of your video ads, commented or liked ads... on a 90-day window)

The following formats perform best:

- UGC from real clients (success stories // testimonials)
- Big Result with social proof (timeline + mechanism)
- Before / After case studies

Prospects might be thinking, 'this is too good to be true'.
Show them it actually works.


3. CLOSE THE DEAL (Bottom of Funnel)

They've seen your ads & your content.
They watched your demo or your VSL.
They looked into your pricing.

It's time to double down.

Retarget these hot leads (30-day window, 75% video views, contact/pricing page visits) with:

- Direct CTA Ads (offer + what they'll get from talking to you)
- Testimonial Ads (short quote + success metrics)

text:
AI Agents are replacing employees.

Some companies even trust them with corporate credit cards.

We're seeing this disruption across all departments.

And by 2027, it's predicted that ~80% will adopt them.

That said, in many cases, what we believe is an AI agent... is just a clever workflow.

Let's look at a typical work task to illustrate this, via 3 scenarios.

For example:

→ Scheduling a quarterly business review with a major client.


A. Non-Agentic Workflows

Humans handle all the work, and leverage tools that act based on their instructions:

1. A manager remembers it's time for the business review.

2. They check their calendar and their CRM.

3. They ask ChatGPT to "draft an email to schedule a client call"

4. They complete the draft and send the email.

Human did all the thinking.
AI didn't take any initiative.
It just helped with content.


B. Agentic Workflow

AI is part of a system with automated triggers & logic.

1. A calendar automation gets triggered as it's been 90 days since the latest business review.

2. The automation checks for availability in the calendar of the manager.

3. The automation then triggers the drafting of an email to schedule a meeting.

4. The email is automatically sent.

The workflow is semi-autonomous.
It saves time... 

But won't adapt to unexpected scenarios (i.e: follow-up, rescheduling)


C. AI Agents

The Agent has a 'goal-oriented objective'.

In this case: "Keep client happy & engaged".

1. Agent constantly checks CRM, activity & past clients' conversations.

2. It detects it's time for the quarterly business review. It also checks billing tier & checks recent usage drop.

3. It drafts a personalized note ('Hey Maïa, I see your team recently added 4 users, but they don't seem to use the platform that much...") and suggests times to meet.

4. It sends the email and monitors replies. It'll automatically follow up to suggest more time slots if it doesn't get an answer within 2-5 days.

5; Once the meeting is set, it comes up with an agenda based on previous convos, and warns the CS team of potential red flags (i.e: low usage → high churn risk)

It coordinates multiple tools.
It's contextual & personalised.

It focuses on a 'bigger goal' (i.e, client satisfaction) instead of a 'small task' (i.e, drafting & sending an email).

P.S.: Are you automating your repetitive work with AI at the moment?

What are you tackling in priority? 👇

→ Cold Email: Low = Built for direct conversion.


7. Deliverability

→ Cold Email: Around ~60 to 70% if set up correctly. Spam risk is high.


8. Average reply rate

→ WhatsApp: ~30%

→ Cold Email: 1-10%

text:

→ LinkedIn: Booking meetings by publishing relevant snackable content.

→ YouTube: Building trust & booking meetings via in-depth educational videos.


2. Key Rules to Win

LinkedIn: 

A. Find outlier/viral/proven publications using tools like Taplio.
B. Consistent high-quality posts relevant to your ICP.
C. Frequent engagement actions with your audience.
D. Optimized profile (banner, title, featured section).

YouTube:

A. Nail combination of thumbnail + title before recording.
B. Focus on quality. YouTube = "Winner takes all"
C. Deep research on titles, thumbnails & trends.


3. Posting Time & Frequency

→ LinkedIn: 3 to 7 posts per week. Same posting time every day.

→ YouTube: 1 video per week. Posting when audience is most online.


4. Top Software

→ LinkedIn:

- Content Ideation + Analytics: Taplio
- Visuals: Figma, Canva, OpusClip
- Writing: Claude, Grammarly

→ YouTube:

- Content Ideation: 1of10, Viewstats, vidIQ
- Production: Adobe Premiere Suite
- Recording: Tella, OBS Studio


5. Expected Reach

→ LinkedIn:

- Audience = B2B focused (i.e: sales, marketing, HR & tech buyers).
- Prospects browse the feed to educate or entertain themselves.
- Over 310,000,000 monthly active users.

→ YouTube:

- Audience = Broad, top-of-funnel (creators, entrepreneurs, founders).
- Audience is actively searching for the content you're creating.
- Over 2,500,000,000 monthly active users.


6. Engagement Expectation

→ LinkedIn: 

- Decent conversion rate. 'Easy' to produce content scale.
- You can reach out to post engagers (DMs).
- Leads are nurtured daily.

→ YouTube:

- High conversion rate from long-form content.
- Audience can binge-watch channels.
- Can't contact viewers directly.


7. Challenges

→ LinkedIn:

- Can take weeks/months before generating any leads.
- Staying consistent is hard.

→ YouTube:

- Lots of upfront work to get 1 good video out.
- Consequent investment in studio setup.
- Talking to a camera can feel weird.


If you had to pick one platform to scale your business, which would you choose?

Why do I want to grow these numbers further?

↳ Just last month, we added $89,000+ MRR from new 13 deals. LinkedIn was responsible for 8 of them. And I’d argue it positively influenced the remaining 5.

Having multiple people share their POV on LinkedIn exposes prospects to so many content pieces… that by the time they talk to our sales team, they’re already half sold.

Last month, we collectively published 233 posts.

I believe we can reach 500 by end of year… without sacrificing quality.


Here’s what’s worked best for us so far in 2025:


1. Leveraging platforms like Taplio for content ideation

It lets you find publications that outperformed.

It’s the fastest way to understand what ‘good’ posts look like for LinkedIn.

Study hooks, frameworks, formats, and CTAs of all these posts.

Re-use the structure of these ‘winning’ publications, and apply them to your niche.


2. Engaging with other creators

LinkedIn pushes you much more when you actively comment on others’ posts.

Last year, I read an experiment where someone:

- Only commented for a couple of weeks
- Only posted for 2 weeks
- Posted & commented

Obviously, posting & commenting together drove the most profile views and follower growth.

But, interestingly, commenting alone earned them more followers than just posting.

Try commenting under posts from large creators, and look at the impression metrics. These might be higher than on any of your posts.

Also, to boost your posts, try this:
- Comment on others’ posts 30 min before hitting ‘publish’
- Reply to every comment you get within the first 30 minutes.


3. Creating scroll-stopping visuals

Visuals occupy lots of space on the LinkedIn feed.

This significantly improves the odds that people read your posts.

Selfies, schemas, infographics, carousels… all these will multiply the reach of your posts.

We’re making it as easy as possible for our team thanks to our designers (Clara & Ada).


4. Repurposing your best hits

Every couple of months: Have a look at your best-performing posts… and rewrite them slightly better.

Have a look at the biggest LinkedIn content creators.

Check their most viral posts.

You’ll notice, they’ve published them over and over…
And they keep performing!

Most viewers forget your posts.
New followers never saw them.

So take your best post ever.
And publish it again.


P.S: Don’t be shocked by the male-to-female ratio in the picture… we have 8 amazing women working with us (who were either hidden or couldn’t make it in time for this team’s off-site) 😅

text:
LinkedIn's reach is at an all-time low. The posts I publish at 55,000 followers reach fewer people than when I had 30K. But we book more meetings than ever on the platform. Here’s how:

There are 7 people above 8K followers in our team: Me (55K), Alex (50K), Ivan (17K), Soheil (11K), Gerardo (11K), Millie (9K), Monika (8.5K).

The goal? Expand our Founder-Led Content playbook to grow to 10 people over 10,000 followers.

The fastest-growing accounts in our team all do this:


1. They study high-performing posts

Each fast-growing team member spent time studying viral posts in our niche.

The process typically looks like so:

A. Sign up for Taplio or Scripe
B. Search for posts by topic.
C. Filter posts with >250 likes.

Many fail on LinkedIn because they don’t have a standard to strive for. 

Seeing what works is the fastest way to understand how to optimise your posts.


2. They leverage visual assets

Our designers help our team create visually appealing infographics.

These visuals are effective because they take up the whole space on the feed (and can serve as a second hook).

Nowadays, LinkedIn pushes carousels more than other formats.


3. They find winning formats to be reused weekly

LinkedIn rewards you when you show up 3+ times a week. But coming up with new post ideas is challenging.

The key to making LinkedIn work is to find ‘winning formats’ that you can replicate.

For example, I share weekly:

- Infographics breaking down how we hit internal milestones:
   
  → specific # of visitors on our site
  → amount of new MRR added
  → # of LinkedIn followers
   
- Likewise, I’ll regularly share a carousel of tools in a specific GTM category. 

E.g:
→ ‘Best B2B data sources’ or ‘Best Scraping tools’

The overarching format is the same, but the content changes. 

Thus, you can post frequently, without repeating yourself.


4. They repurpose their best-performing content

Your LinkedIn posts are forgotten within 48 hours.

If you publish the same piece a month later, people will have forgotten, and others won’t have seen it.

So, for example, every 2 months, I share my favourite cold email templates from sales creators.

But instead of just publishing it, I’ll find another 1-2 that I discovered recently.

So what started as my “5 favourite cold email templates” turned into my “7 favourite templates”, and later on, into my “10 favourites”.

The angle of the post is proven, and I add to it, which makes it more valuable, without requiring too much effort on my part.


5. They leverage tech

E.g: 
- Notion to plan their content calendar
- Taplio or Scripe to identify winning posts
- Grammarly to correct their spelling in real-time
- OpusClip to turn their videos into short-form clips

text:
I ran my first outbound campaign 7 years ago. Then, grew a cold email agency from 0 to $6,000,000+ ARR in the last 2. Here are 7 things I wish I knew before starting:

1. Most of your time should be spent on your lead list

Sending outreach messages to the right person matters more than anything else.

So...
→ Precisely figure out what problem you're solving.
→ Find companies struggling with this problem.
→ Identify relevant individuals in these orgs.


2. Provide as much value or insights as you can

You're interrupting people's days by sending them unsolicited messages.

Providing value, or great insights, is the fastest way to build trust with your prospects. 

One way I like to do so is by:
→ Reflecting on what I'll do first when I sign my prospect.
→ Doing it already.
→ Giving it away for free.


3. Write for 1 person, before attempting to write for 1,000.

Most orgs build massive lead lists, and then try to write copy that appeals to every single person in their list.

Appealing to everyone = appealing to no one.

Thus, do the opposite.

Find 1 ideal lead, and write as if they where the only person in your world.

Then...

→ Find 10-20 others, and repeat the process.
→ You'll uncover patterns among your leads.
→ Then, automate sending on a bigger scale.


4. Properly set up your deliverability

Good deliverability doesn't guarantee your campaigns will succeed. But...
Bad deliverability guarantees your campaigns will fail.

Make sure to...

→ Send few emails per mailbox (< 30 per day)
→ Set up DMARK, SPF, DKIM records.
→ Disable open tracking.
→ Warm up mailboxes.


5. Make the EXTRA effort

Cold email is a hard channel to crack. You want to go the extra mile:

→ Don't just target job titles or company sizes. Look at triggers, signals, current events, org. charts.
→ Don't just look a new jobs openings. Read & scan job descriptions.
→ Don't stop at 1-2 email variations. Write 5+


6. Pair outbound with other channels.

Cold Email is my favourite channel to get started with.
But it works even better with other channels.

E.g:

→ Use cold emails to distribute valuable lead magnets.
→ Run ads to the same people you're cold emailing.
→ Make content, and reach out to 'engagers'


7. Leverage technology

"A fool with a tool is still a fool"

But the right tech will make you more efficient.

→ Have a look at ColdIQ's directory of sales tools :)
→ Review repetitive processes that could be automated.
→ Before hiring more headcount, ask yourself "could I do this with tech?"


P.S: How are your cold email campaigns doing at the moment?

text:
How to get a 30%+ response rate with LinkedIn DMs:

(Based on > 200 pitches I got last week in my inbox)

For context, I sent 10,000,000+ prospecting messages this year for my $6,000,000+ ARR outbound agency.

Now, I spend more time cleaning my inbox than running campaigns.

I'm the Founder & CEO of a 34-person company.
And I know many execs check their inbox, and reply to cold DMs.

Here's how I decide whether I'll respond or ignore you...
And how I adapted my own cold pitches ↓


✅ DMs that offer *free* work

I've gotten DMs offering to rewrite my site's landing pages, write sample scripts for my YouTube channel.

With ColdIQ, we ran campaigns giving away lead lists...
And we got way more replies than we knew to do with.

Pro tip: Imagine you already signed your prospect as client. What would you do first for them? Do it already, and give it away.


✅ DMs that ask for an internal referral

Let's say you researched current initiatives we're running at ColdIQ, and you identified the person who 'owns' it.

I'll happily refer you the right person.

Pro tip: With Clay, you can 'scale' this play by mixing buying signals with their 'find person' feature to retrieve a colleague based on a department.

(Also, my friend Brahim at LeadsFactory built a 'find person' feature that catches contacts that Clay misses, check it out!)


❌ DMs asking to 'pick' my brain

I frequently receive DMs from tech builders & entrepreneurs that want my opinion on what they're building. 

I'd love to but time is scarce... and there's nothing in it for me.


✅ DMs that share valuable insights

I published a similar post a time ago, and got a great insight from Jihad Iqbal, which is worth sharing 👇

"
The best "free work" isn't actually work. It's insights.

I send technical audits of prospects' platforms.
→ 5-minute analysis
→ 3 specific optimization opportunities 
→ No strings attached

E.g: "Your checkout flow has a 23% drop-off at payment verification. Here's why + 2 quick fixes."

- Takes me 10 minutes.
- Shows immediate value.
- Demonstrates expertise without asking for anything.

The key: Make it so valuable they'd normally pay for it.

Generic "free consultation" = everyone does this.
Specific actionable insight = rare.
"

Definitely a winning approach ☝️


❌ DMs without an ounce of personalization

Many organizations still rely on mass volume, sending the same teamplate to about everyone.

Appealing to everyone = appealing to no one.

So you're most likely wasting DMs. 


✅ DMs from ‘notorious’ people

Perhaps more unfair, but WHO sends the message matters as much as the message itself.

Imagine Alex Hormozi sending you the worst LinkedIn DM ever... would you reply? I would.

I saw my own response rates increases in direct relation to my follower growth.

Pro tip: If your prospects scroll LinkedIn, build your personal brand.

text:
LinkedIn DM vs. Cold Email:

What books more meetings?

I ran cold email for 150+ companies and grew my outbound agency to > $6M ARR. 

But Stefan Smulders, the Co-Founder of Expandi.io, grew his LinkedIn tool to $10M and believes LinkedIn is better...

So we made a side-by-side comparison 👇

1/ Core Focus

→ Cold Email: Book direct meetings with your ideal clients.
→ LinkedIn DMs: Start conversations & nurture existing leads.


2/ Limits

→ Cold Email: Max. 40 emails per day, per mailbox.
→ LinkedIn: Max. 100 weekly DMs or connection requests, per account.


3/ How to win

→ Cold Email:

1. Deliver value in the most concise possible way.
2. Implement a reliable deliverability engine.
3. Research every prospect.
4. Showcase social proof.

→ LinkedIn:

1. Be active on the platform (i.e: posts + comments on top of DMs)
2. Personalize outreach based on prospects' social activities.
3. Optimize LinkedIn profile.


4/ Technology to use

→ Cold Email: Instantly.ai, lemlist
→ LinkedIn: Expandi.io


5/ Who to sell to

→ Cold Email: Any person who opens emails.
→ LinkedIn: Tech Roles, Sellers, Marketers, HRs, B2B Execs.


6/ Expectations

→ Cold Email: Low reply rates. 'Easy' to scale volume through secondary mailboxes setup.

→ LinkedIn: High(er) reply rates. 'Tougher' to scale if you have a small team.


7/ Typical challenges

→ Cold Email: Landing in spam. Competing in crowded inboxes.

→ LinkedIn: Account restrictions when you take too many actions (# of DMs or connection requests).


So are you team Cold Email, team LinkedIn... or both?

text:
Before growing ColdIQ to > $500k/mo:


I started and grew an affiliate sports betting site to 6K€/mo.

→ Belgium changed its regulation around offering bonuses for gambling, and my site went to 0 overnight.


I invested £40k to start a raffle lottery in the UK 🇬🇧

→ I sold around £1K worth of lottery tickets. The rest of the money? All gone.


I started a streetwear clothing brand with Thibault Selderslagh.

→ We sold less than 15 t-shirts. Minimal production order was 400. So there are 385 left, collecting dust somewhere.


I tried to become an Instagram influencer.

→ Found a ‘hack’ on Instagram’s algorithm. Grew to > 30,000+ followers. Instagram found out. Made sure people couldn’t use the hack anymore. I’ve lost followers everyday ever since.


I launched a Facebook Ads agency.

→ I booked 15 sales meetings. I didn’t close a single one.


I started an MMA betting blog AND a crypto blog

→ They generated less than $1 combined.


Also, I almost forgot, I managed to get fired from 3 different jobs.

→ I deserved it. Every single time.


As I went from failure to failure… I’d often wonder why things couldn’t be easier.

Back then, I didn’t understand I needed to go through these, to grow a 7-figure business.

Because each failure taught me something I use today for my business:

- I learned copywriting thanks to my failed blogs (a skill I use every day to generate leads from LinkedIn)

- I learned how to monetize partnerships thanks to my failed betting sports website (affiliate generates us multi 5-figures per month in revenue)

- I learned ads thanks to my failed lottery (which is now an additional offering & revenue stream for us).

- I learned cold emails trying to book meetings for my failed Facebook ads agency (which ultimately gave birth to ColdIQ, my most successful venture so far)

The takeaway here is that you need to keep trying.

The US SaaS Market is worth ~225B. Europe’s ‘only’ at ~$95B. But in 2025, the best Tech isn’t coming from Silicon Valley anymore.

Take Sales Tech. This market alone shall hit $141B by 2030. And, admittedly, the biggest organisations (HubSpot, ZoomInfo, Outreach, Salesforce, LinkedIn) all come from the US.

That said, I’ll argue, some of the best breakout stories in recent years came from Europe.

Here are some of my favourites:

1/ Attio 🇬🇧

Born out of London, Attio is revolutionising the CRM space, with their AI-native & automation-heavy approach. Not an easy task, with Hubspot & Salesforce dominating the industry for over 20 years.

But teams are increasingly switching to Attio (including ourselves, at ColdIQ!).
And the momentum is real, with them raising a $52M series B just yesterday.

Not sure about their current revenue, but they quadrupled their ARR in 2025 already.

Stay tuned…


2/ Instantly.ai 🇪🇪

Born between Estonia & India, Instantly went after Sales Engagement giants with a simple, yet powerful value proposition: “scale your email sending, without scaling your costs”.

When every platform forced you to pay per seat for any new user, Instantly democratised email outreach at scale to smaller teams with smaller budgets.

Some say it created ‘too much’ spam in the space. I say, big-budget organisations were just mad to find out that smaller teams could now compete with them volume-wise.

They never share revenue numbers publicly, but I estimate them to be well above $20M ARR given their number of users.


3/ FullEnrich 🇫🇷

0 → $1.8M ARR on year 1.
$1.8M ARR → > $5M ARR already in year 2.

The numbers speak for themselves.

Their software aggregates the best email & phone number finders in one place.
It’s ColdIQ’s #1 platform to find phone numbers.


4/ Expandi.io 🇳🇱

Born in Holland, Expandi is the OG of LinkedIn outreach.

They’ve grown to $10M ARR, completely bootstrapped, by sharing valuable tips on LinkedIn outreach and building one of the most comprehensive sales engagement solution in the space.


5/ lemlist 🇫🇷

Most probably the most notorious French success story in Sales Tech. 
lempire is a > $34M ARR umbrella company that includes lemlist, Taplio, Tweet Hunter and lemcal.

Even more notorious than their product itself, their branding/marketing has always been one step ahead.

If you want to use a great multi-channel outreach platform, use lemlist.
If you want to build a successful product in the GTM space, study lemlist’s growth playbook.


There are a ton of other cool EU success stories, such as Genesy 🇪🇸, Aircall 🇫🇷, Ocean.io 🇩🇰, Pipedrive 🇫🇷, Crono 🇮🇹, Prospeo.io 🇫🇷, Twain 🇩🇪, HeyReach.io 🇲🇰 , Breakcold 🇫🇷, Reply🇺🇦 , PhantomBuster 🇫🇷, Bizzy 🇧🇪 & plenty more…

text:
The #1 thing to address if your cold emails don't get replies:

(and it's easier to fix than you'd think)

→ EMAIL DELIVERABILITY

Here are 5 steps to fix it ASAP:

1️⃣ Build an email infrastructure.

= Purchase secondary mailboxes & domains.

That's essential, since sending too many emails from your main domain might get it flagged. 

The consequence = critical comms, such as client invoicing emails landing in spam. You might get away with it... but best not to take the risk altogether.

→ You can build your infrastructure through Instantly.ai done-for-you email setup or outsource to ColdIQ.


2️⃣ Warm up your domains/mailboxes 

Fresh mailboxes are suspicious to the eyes of the email service providers (ESP).

New inboxes are often used for phishing, so the first emails you send to them are more likely to land in SPAM.

The fix = adding these inboxes to a warm-up pool, where sent emails that land in spam are removed and flagged as 'safe'. Do that enough times, and ESPs will believe your emails deserve to be out of SPAM.

Then, start sending actual cold emails, and slowly increase sending volume.

→ Any solid sales engagement platform (i.e: lemlist, Instantly.ai) includes warm-up features that will improve your domain's reputation.


3️⃣ Clean your target lists.

Every time you send an email that bounces, you're sending a bad signal to email platforms.

Think about it: if you know the email address of the person you're sending a message to... how likely are you to miswrite their contact information?

Pretty low... right?

Well this is how email platforms 'guess' that you're sending unsolicited emails... and it greatly improves your odds of landing in spam.

→ Make sure to use reputable tools to validate (& find) email contact data. Examples include: LeadMagic, FullEnrich, Prospeo.io.


4️⃣ Optimize your copy

A few tweaks in your copy will greatly improve your odds of landing outside of spam.

That is, using:
- spintax = random wording variation so you never send the same 'template'
- no links = avoid adding unnecessary URLs to your emails
- plain text = writing 'without' fancy formatting

... and don't track your open rates.


5️⃣ Most important: Send emails you'd want to receive

You need to remember you're sending unsolicited outreach messages.

Prospects are receiving a ton already.

If you provide great value, you can break some of the above rules... and you will do just fine!

P.S: How are your cold email campaigns performing this month? Not too many Out-of-Office replies?

Campaigns with copy tailored to the ICP got up to 54.7% more replies.

→ Take some time to personalize your messages; it'll go a long way.


2. Short > Long

Messages under 150 characters had 22% more replies on average.

→ Aim to get your point across in as few words as possible.


3. Contextual > Generic

Messages referencing a recent activity (i.e: a LinkedIn post, a change in role) saw +18% replies.

→ Find a relevant reason to reach out.


4. Warm approach > Cold approach

Connection requests sent after:
- profile visits
- post likes
- follows

... saw a +30.2% acceptance rate.

→ Make yourself seen, before reaching out.


5. 3-Step Sequence > 1 Single Message

Sequences with 3+ steps performed 42% better than single-message flows.

→ Don't be afraid to follow up.


6. Multi-Channel > Single Channel

Adding an email follow-up after not getting a reply on LinkedIn lifted reply rates by 13.8%.

→ Don't rely on LinkedIn only.


7. Conversationnal Copy > Direct Pitches

Examples:

[+ 18.2% replies] Trigger-Based Hook: "Noticed you're hiring {role} - what's working for you?"

[+ 19.3% replies] Post reference: "Saw your post on {topic}, curious what are you testing right now?"

[+ 21.5% replies] Job change hook: "Saw you joined {company} - how's the first month going so far?"

[+ 27.1% replies] Peer Comparison in the CTA: "We analyzed {findings on topic} - worth sharing what others in your space are doing?"


8. Key Metrics to track

- Acceptance rate: Aim for > 40%.

- Reply rate: Aim for > 18%.

- Positive reply rate: Aim for > 8%.


9. Tech Stack

- Expandi.io (sequencing, automation, routing, analytics)

- LinkedIn Sales Navigator (list building, targeting, filtering)

text:
I went from 0 to 50,000+ LinkedIn followers. In the process, I booked 2,000+ meetings, signed 150+ B2B clients & 300+ coaching customers for ColdIQ. Here's how I did it:

It took 3 attempts to succeed at publishing consistently... & I had to post 30+ times before getting my 1st lead. 

If you’re considering posting here, here’s why you should absolutely do it, and how to succeed:

WHY YOU MUST POST:

1. You’re still early. As Noam Nisand points out in his posts, just 1% of people regularly post on LinkedIn. (vs 34% on X, 25% on Instagram & 20% on Facebook).

2. It’s free advertising, truly. You type a few words, hit a ‘button’, and now all of a sudden 1000s of people are reading your thoughts. Obviously, you need to get your way up to these numbers. Which, for us, is > 20M impressions, which, at a $30 CPM, would’ve cost $600,000 in ads for the same amount of eyeballs.

3. It enhances all other marketing efforts. My outreach campaign results 3X’d as I gained more followers. People check you out on social media. Some know about you before you message them.

4. It can book lots of (> 100/mo) high-paying leads. And some don’t even need to be sold to in the calls. They’ve been exposed to so much content that they’re sold already.

Ok but…

HOW TO MAKE IT WORK?!

1. Go as in-depth as possible. You get less likes than if you were to post memes, but your content translates to better opportunities. Some creators make less monthly revenue than they have followers. If you play your cards well, the opposite should happen. Look at how Gal Aga writes, it’s long, deep, valuable… so it converts.

2. Study what great posts look like. Tools like Taplio & Scripe help you find top-performing content. Study hooks, format, visuals, length and style of these posts. Take inspiration. Don’t copy.

3. Invest resources in great visuals. Posts with (nice) designs get pushed to 3-5X more people. Visuals take lots of space on the feed, can serve as a second hook, and if they’re good enough… can be posts on their own. Check out Ada Beltrán, Pierre Herubel & Nick Broekema for what great visuals look like.

4. Repurpose your best pieces. 6 of my most viewed posts are infographic breaking down our Tech Stack. It’s nearly the same, but reached > 100,000 impressions each time. Most forget your initial post. New followers haven’t even seen it. Test it for yourself: take your best post. Publish it again. It’ll likely perform just as well as the 1st time. 

Quick Tip: Slightly rework/improve the post every time you re-publish it.

5. Take pride in your consistency. Building an audience takes time, and you most likely won’t make any money from the platform in the beginning. Be patient. View it as a trust-building mechanism before it becomes a reliable lead generation machine.

6. Connect with your ICP. They’ll see your content. Imagine what'll happen when 100s of your ideal clients regularly read how you can solve their problems.

I ran out of space. 
More tips in the comments ↓

text:
We deploy this Clay table to every client at our $6M GTM agency

...to 3X the amount of prospects they can reach.

With 75+ B2B clients, things can quickly get messy.

Tools aren't always in sync.
Blocklists are forgotten.

And every single GTM Engineer has their 'unique style' when it comes to building lists.

So, Louis Van Wyk & Shubham Sandilya decided it was about time we fixed this issue...

And built one Clay table, a "master prospecting engine", to be used by every GTME at ColdIQ.

Here's the step-by-step breakdown:

1️⃣ It starts with the Blocklist

We ask every client for a "do-not-contact" list.

This typically is a mix of:

- past clients
- competitors
- existing clients
- or simply companies they don't want to prospect.

The table automatically:

1. Cleans the list.
2. Enriches domain URLs from company names.
3. Blocks any enrichment across every tool for these domains (to save Clay credits)


2️⃣ We find leads from several data sources

This master Clay table:

1. Grabs domains from Ocean.io, DiscoLike, and custom databases (can be via Instant Data Scraper).

2. Import domains to Apollo to find individual contacts and get back the data through Clay's Webhook.

3. Clay then finds more leads from the same domain (no dupes).

4. Prospeo.io enriches additional data from LinkedIn Sales Navigator to find even more leads (still no dupes).

5. All leads, pulled via Webhook, are imported into Clay.


3️⃣ We enrich leads using several providers.

Still, within the table:

1. We find verified emails using Prospeo.io, LeadMagic, FullEnrich.

2. If needed, we find mobile phones through FullEnrich.

3. We fact-check their personal LinkedIn profiles to ensure the person still works there.


4️⃣ We verify emails & phone numbers.

1. Email validation using LeadMagic & Instantly.ai.

2. Phone validation using FullEnrich.


5️⃣ The table is ready to go

The final output: every contact is cleaned & the table is ready to be exported.

We made sure to:
- dedupe every single contact
- validate their information
- sort them by seniority
- get the top 3 per org

... and it can now be pushed to Instantly.ai, lemlist or Expandi.io.

As our team grew past 30 people, this is the best way we found to keep quality high, and chaos low.

It's built once. 
It can be reused, over and over, for every single client.


P.S: If this was valuable, you NEED to follow Louis & Shubham on here. Rumours say they're planning to share some insane table buildouts 👀
